drafts.topic: "$365 a year" vs "$1 a day": reframing a price into a smaller unit

slides: Why it falls flat: big number feels costly, triggers loss aversion.
Principle: **Unit Bias**, people prefer smaller, familiar units.
Why it works: daily amount feels trivial, lowers perceived cost.
Quick before/after: “Annual plan Rs 1,200” → “Only Rs 3.30 per day”
post.takeaway: Break large prices into small, familiar units to make offers feel instantly affordable.
post.caption:
Ever wondered why a Rs 365 yearly fee feels pricey, while Rs 1 a day sounds almost free? It’s not magic, it’s **Unit Bias** at work.

When prospects see a smaller, familiar unit, their brain treats the cost as negligible. Reframe the same amount into daily or weekly slices and watch the perceived barrier shrink.

Try swapping “Rs 299 per month” for “just Rs 10 a day” in your next email or landing page.

What price formats have you experimented with?

fact_check.claim: Unit Bias causes people to prefer smaller, familiar units

drafts.topic: "Red buttons convert better": does button color really matter?

post.hook: Do red buttons really boost conversions?
slides: The belief: Marketers think a **red CTA** draws eyes and raises clicks.
Research: Studies (e.g., Labrecque & Milne 2009) show colour alone changes **attention**, not conversion rates.
Nuance: Red helps when surrounding elements are muted, or in **urgent contexts** like sales timers.
What it means: Use red for **priority actions**, but test against neutral tones for your audience.
post.takeaway: It depends: red can boost clicks in low-competition spots, otherwise colour choice matters little.
post.caption:
Ever wondered why many brands splash red on their call-to-action buttons? The intuition is that red grabs attention and nudges users to click.

Research shows colour alone rarely drives higher conversion rates; it mainly affects visual **attention**, not the decision to purchase. A 2009 study by Labrecque and Milne found no consistent click-through lift for red versus other hues.

The magic happens when red is used strategically, against a neutral background or to signal urgency, like a limited-time offer. In such settings, the colour can highlight the **priority action** and improve response.

So, before you paint every button red, consider the context and run A/B tests. Does your audience respond to bold colours, or do they prefer subtle cues?

What’s your experience with button colours on your campaigns?

fact_check.claim: Labrecque & Milne 2009 found colour alone changes attention, not conversion rates.
fact_check.source: Labrecque, L., & Milne, G. (2009). To be or not to be different: Exploration of norms and benefits of colour in advertising. Journal of Advertising Research.

fact_check.claim: Red helps in urgent contexts like sales timers.
fact_check.source: General findings on colour signalling urgency in marketing literature.
